property_summary: For any caller and any deposit amount >= MinSum, after calling Put(...) the caller's recorded balance in c.Acc(caller).balance equals the sent value added to their prior balance (no unexpected extra deductions via reentrancy); the mutant that removes the require(!locked_) allows reentrant Put to be invoked while locked_, causing the stored balance to differ for some inputs (reentrant attacker contract).

After any external Put call completes, the caller's recorded Acc balance equals the sum of prior balance plus msg.value (no extra increments from reentrant nested Put); removing require(!locked_) allows a reentrant attacker to call Put during the outer Put and cause the final stored balance to be larger, violating that invariant for some inputs.

For any caller and any admissible deposit, a completed Put(...) call always leaves c.Acc(caller).unlockTime >= block.timestamp (i.e., unlockTime is never set to a past timestamp); the mutant allowing reentrancy can cause a reentrant Put to run with block.timestamp still the same and set unlockTime differently so that after completion this property can be violated for some inputs.

For every caller and any deposit amount and unlockTime, calling Put(...) on the correct contract never reverts (completes successfully); the mutant that removes the require(!locked_) can be exploited by a reentrant attacker causing an internal reentrancy that makes Put revert (or behave differently) for some inputs, so we assert Put succeeds on the reference for all fuzzed inputs while the mutant can fail for some.

For any caller, any deposit amount and any unlockTime, a call to Put(...) on the correct contract always succeeds (does not revert); removing the require(!locked_) allows a reentrant malicious fallback to invoke Put reentrantly and cause an internal state that makes the outer call revert for some inputs, so the reference always returns ok=true while the mutant can produce ok=false.

The nonReentrant_ modifier in the correct contract always allows an external call to Put when the contract is unlocked (require(!locked_)), so calling Put from any EOA should succeed (not revert) for any caller and value; the mutant inverts the require to require(locked_) which will make Put revert for callers when locked_ is false, so some fuzzed inputs (caller/value) will cause Put to revert in the mutant but not in the reference.

For every caller and ether amount, calling Put(...) should succeed on the reference (contract starts unlocked) but the mutant that requires(locked_) will revert for some caller/value combinations (specifically any call when locked_ is false), so the reference never reverts while the mutant sometimes does.

For any caller and any Ether amount, calling Put(...) on the reference C (which starts unlocked) never reverts (Put always succeeds); the mutant inverts the reentrancy guard check so Put will revert when locked_ is false, causing some calls to fail.

For any caller address and any positive ether value, calling Put(...) on the reference C (which starts unlocked) does not revert (call succeeds); the mutant inverts the reentrancy require and can make Put revert when locked_ is false, so some inputs cause Put to fail in the mutant.

For any caller address and any uint256 value, calling Put(...) with that caller sending that ether amount to the reference contract always succeeds (does not revert) because locked_ starts false; the mutant inverts the require to require(locked_) and therefore will revert for calls when locked_ is false, breaking this rule for some inputs.

Reference contract always preserves the depositor's balance decrease only when an external transfer (call) to the depositor succeeds (i.e., after Put+Collect sequence the stored balance reflects successful outgoing payments), but the mutant which clears locked_ before the external call can allow the external call to re-enter and cause inconsistent balance changes (leading to a different final stored balance for some inputs).

After a Put by any depositor, the depositor's recorded balance in Acc[msg] must equal the sum of all deposits they made (i.e., Put never decreases stored balance); the mutant that clears locked_ early can be re-entered during an external call and thereby make the stored balance inconsistent for some inputs.

For any depositor and any deposit amount >= MinSum, after a single Put(...) call the contract's recorded Acc[depositor].balance increases by exactly the sent value (Put never causes a decrease or reentrant side-effect); the mutant that clears the reentrancy lock before the function body allows a reentrant Collect() during Put and can make Acc[depositor].balance differ (fail this invariant) for some inputs.

After any single Put call from an address, that caller's recorded Acc balance is at least the amount they just sent (Put never results in a net decrease of the caller's stored balance); the mutant that clears locked_ before the function body can be re-entered during Put and may cause the caller's stored balance to be less than the just-sent amount for some inputs.

For any depositor and any deposit amount >= MinSum, calling Put(...) always results in the depositor's recorded Acc[depositor].balance increasing by exactly the sent value (Put does not allow reentrant Collect to run during Put and so cannot reduce the just-added balance); the mutant that clears locked_ before the function body permits reentrant Collect during Put and can make Acc[depositor].balance smaller than the sent amount for some inputs.

After any successful Put(amount, unlockTime) by an account, the contract's recorded Acc(account).unlockTime is always at least the block.timestamp (i.e., cannot be set to a past time); the mutant allowing unconditional assignment of _unlockTime can store a value < block.timestamp for some fuzzed _unlockTime and thus violates this rule.

For any caller and any Put(...) call, the contract C records Acc(caller).unlockTime >= block.timestamp (it never stores a past unlock time); the mutant that assigns _unlockTime unconditionally can store a value < block.timestamp and thus violate this invariant for some fuzzed _unlockTime.

After any Put called by any actor with any value and any _unlockTime, the contract's stored Acc(actor).unlockTime is always >= the block.timestamp at the moment Put returned; the mutant that assigns _unlockTime unconditionally can store a value < block.timestamp for some fuzzed _unlockTime and thus violates this invariant.

For every caller and any inputs, after Put returns the stored Acc(caller).unlockTime is either the supplied _unlockTime when that is >= block.timestamp, or else block.timestamp (i.e., stored unlockTime >= min(_unlockTime, block.timestamp)); the mutant that unconditionally assigns _unlockTime can produce stored unlockTime < block.timestamp for some inputs, violating this rule.

For every caller, after calling Put(_unlockTime) the stored Acc(caller).unlockTime equals either the provided _unlockTime when it is in the future, or else block.timestamp — i.e., stored unlockTime >= block.timestamp (the reference enforces a non-past stored unlockTime); the mutant that assigns unconditionally can store a value < block.timestamp for some fuzzed _unlockTime and thus violates this.

For any caller and any msg.value and _unlockTime, calling Put(...) increases the caller's recorded Acc[msg.sender].balance by msg.value (so Acc[msg.sender].balance_after == balance_before + msg.value); the mutant that omits updating acc.balance violates this for some inputs (nonzero msg.value).

For any caller and any nonzero msg.value, after calling Put(_unlockTime) the caller's recorded Acc[msg.sender].balance increases by exactly msg.value (reference preserves this invariant; the mutant that omits updating acc.balance violates it for some inputs).

For every caller and any sent ETH amount, after calling Put(...) the contract's public Acc[msg.sender].balance increases by exactly the sent msg.value (the correct contract updates acc.balance; the mutant that deletes the update will violate this for some nonzero msg.value).

For any actor and any sent ETH amount, calling Put records the received ETH in the contract's overall balance (address(c).balance increases by msg.value); the mutant that fails to update internal accounting still receives ETH but the observable contract balance behavior remains same — instead instead we target that LogFile.LastMsg.Val equals the msg.value after Put, which the reference sets to msg.value and the mutant also sets — so instead use that the public mapping Acc[msg.sender].balance equals the sum of all prior Put msg.values (i.e., after a sequence: if actor calls Put repeatedly, Acc balance equals cumulative sent); the mutant that omits adding msg.value breaks this for nonzero amounts.

For every caller and any sequence of calls, the contract's public Acc[caller].unlockTime after Put(maxUnlock) equals the maximum of prior unlockTime and the provided _unlockTime (capped at block.timestamp), and the buggy mutant still updates unlockTime the same, so this won't detect it; instead we assert that after Put with nonzero msg.value the contract's overall ether balance increases by msg.value (which the reference satisfies for all inputs) — the mutant still receives ETH too, so that also won't detect it. To detect the mutant that omits updating acc.balance but still logs msg.value, we instead assert that when an actor calls Put and then immediately tries to Collect the same amount (with unlockTime set to past), Collect will only succeed (reduce Acc[actor].balance and send funds) if acc.balance was increased by the Put; thus: for any actor, amount, and unlockTime where unlockTime <= block.timestamp and amount >= MinSum, after vm.prank(actor); c.Put{value:amount}(unlockTime) then trying c.Collect(amount) should succeed iff the contract's Acc[actor].balance before Collect was >= amount — the reference always allows Collect to succeed in this scenario (since Put updated balance), but the mutant causes Collect to revert or not send funds because balance wasn't increased — we express this by calling Collect via try/catch and asserting that it returns true (succeeds) for all inputs, which the reference satisfies and the mutant fails for some inputs.

For any caller and payment amount, calling Put(...) increases the caller's (msg.sender) Acc balance by the sent value; the mutant that updates Acc[tx.origin] instead can leave msg.sender's balance unchanged when msg.sender != tx.origin.

For any caller and payment amount, after calling Put(...) the stored balance for msg.sender increases by the sent value (i.e. Acc(msg.sender).balance == previous + value); the mutant that writes Acc[tx.origin] instead can leave Acc(msg.sender).balance unchanged when msg.sender != tx.origin, so this property is violated for calls where msg.sender != tx.origin (e.g., when a contract calls Put on behalf of an EOA).

For any caller contract A and any send amount, after A calls c.Put(...) the stored Acc[A].balance increases by the amount sent; the mutant that writes Acc[tx.origin] instead can fail this when A (a contract) calls c.Put on behalf of an EOA, leaving Acc[A].balance unchanged.

For any caller contract A (msg.sender) that forwards an EOA's payment to C.Put, Acc[A].balance increases by the forwarded msg.value; the mutant writing to Acc[tx.origin] instead leaves Acc[A].balance unchanged when tx.origin != A, violating this rule.

For any caller contract A that calls C.Put with some ETH, C.Acc(A).balance increases by the sent amount; the mutant that writes to Acc[tx.origin] instead can leave Acc(A).balance unchanged when tx.origin != A (i.e., when an EOA funds through a contract), so the property is violated for such inputs.

After a successful Collect call the caller's recorded Acc[msg.sender].balance equals its previous balance minus the collected amount, even if the recipient's withdrawal fails (i.e., Collect either reduces stored balance when call succeeds or reverts leaving balance unchanged).
